Business plan text:

Tabletop Turnover
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Tabletop Turnover LLC
Problem
Independent restaurants have a big problem with the dinner rush. When the restaurant is full
the host do not know when the tables will be open again, so they quote wait times to guests
that are guesses and are often wrong. When the wait quoted is too long guests leave and go to
another restaurant. When the wait is too short guests get angry because they wait longer than
they was told. Also the host sometimes put a party of two at a table for six and then a party
of six have to wait even though there was a table, which is a waste of seats and revenue. This
problem is very painful for independent restaurants because they have thin margins, usually
five percent or less, and every lost table during the busiest hours of the night is lost money
that they can not get back. Large chains have corporate systems to deal with this but
independent restaurants have only paper, memory and gut feeling. We believe that this is a big
problem that is not solved.
Solution
Tabletop Turnover is desktop software that is installed on the computer at the host stand. The
software use data analytics and machine learning algorithms to predict the table turn time for
every table in the restaurant. It looks at the party size, the time of night, the day of the
week, what the guests ordered, and how long similar parties took before. Then it gives the host
a recommendation of which party to seat at which table and a more accurate wait time to quote
to the guests. The software is simple to use and has a dashboard that shows all the tables in
different colors. Our solution is a game changer because it takes the guessing out of the
dinner rush and optimizes seating to shorten waits. We chose desktop software and not a web app
because many independent restaurants do not have reliable internet at the host stand and they
want to own their data. We have built a prototype of the core prediction engine and the
dashboard.
Market
The restaurant industry in the United States is very large, with hundreds of billions of
dollars in sales every year. There are many hundreds of thousands of restaurants in the country
and a majority of them are independent. If just one percent of independent restaurants would
buy our software at our price we would have a very big business. We think our target market is
the full service independent restaurants with between fifteen and sixty tables that have a wait
during the dinner rush. These restaurants are the best fit because they are busy enough to have
a wait but not large enough to have a big technology budget. We have not done a formal market
study yet but we talked to some restaurant owners and they said the idea is interesting. The
market is growing because restaurants are coming back after the pandemic and more owners are
looking for technology to help them.
Business Model
We will charge a monthly subscription fee per restaurant. We are thinking of between fifty and
one hundred fifty dollars per month but we have not decided the exact price yet. We might also
have a setup fee for installing and connecting the software to the restaurant point of sale
system. In the future we could also sell extra features like reports, staff scheduling
suggestions and a version for restaurants with multiple locations. We could also take a small
percent of the extra revenue we help the restaurant make, which is another possibility. We will
get customers by visiting restaurants in person, by social media, by partnering with restaurant
associations and by word of mouth between owners. Our cost is mostly our own time, some cloud
servers for training the model, and some customer support. We believe our margins will be very
high because software is scalable and once it is built it costs little to add a new customer.

Competition
The space of restaurant technology is crowded and there are many companies that offer
reservation systems, waitlist apps, point of sale systems and table management. Some of these
systems have some features about wait time estimates already. Many of them are well funded and
have big sales teams and thousands of customers. However we think we are different because we
are focused only on the turn time prediction and the seating optimization and because we are
desktop software for independent restaurants who do not want to pay for a big expensive system.
Our competitors are mostly trying to be everything for every restaurant while we do just one
thing very well. We also compete with the status quo, which is a paper chart and an experienced
host, and many owners think that works fine. It is possible that the big competitors could add
our feature easily, which is a risk we know about, but we believe our focus and our algorithm
will keep us ahead.
Team
Devon Kowalczyk is the chief executive officer and is a senior studying business administration
at our university. He worked two summers as a server and one summer as a host at a family
restaurant so he knows the dinner rush problem personally. He is in charge of sales, strategy
and customer discovery.
Marisol Yeboah-Santangelo is the chief technology officer and is a senior studying computer
science with a focus on data science at our university. She built the prototype and the
prediction model. She has experience with Python and data analysis from her classes and from a
research assistant job.
Preston Wuthrich is the chief operating officer and is a junior studying finance at our
university. He is in charge of the financial model, legal matters, and operations. He also
helped to register the company.
We do not yet have an advisor from the restaurant industry but we are looking for one.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two milestones. First, we registered Tabletop Turnover as a limited
liability company. Second, we built a prototype, or minimum viable product, with a working
dashboard and a first version of the prediction model. The model was trained on made up data
that we generated ourselves and on a small sample of sales records that one restaurant owner
shared with us, so we still need to test it with real restaurants in real conditions. We do not
have paying customers or revenue yet and we do not have a website yet. We have spent a small
amount of our own money on legal registration and cloud costs. Our financial projection is that
if we get twenty restaurants in the first year paying one hundred dollars per month we would
have a revenue of twenty four thousand dollars, and then it will grow quickly to many more
restaurants in year two and year three, reaching a profit by year three. These projections are
estimates and they depend on many assumptions that we need to validate.
What We Ask For
We are applying to the business plan competition to get funding, mentorship and visibility for
our startup. If we win prize money we would use it to pay for a pilot with five to ten local
restaurants, to improve the prediction model with real data, to build a simple website, and to
pay for a part of the sales and marketing. We also would like to meet mentors who know the
restaurant industry and who can introduce us to restaurant owners and to investors. We believe
that Tabletop Turnover has the potential to be a big company that disrupt the way independent
restaurants manage their dinner rush, and with the help of this competition we can take the
next step from prototype to real customers.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
**Viability and Scalability of Business Model and Strategy:**

**1. Viability of Business Model:**
- **Revenue Model:** The proposed business model relies on a monthly subscription fee, which is a common and scalable model in SaaS (Software as a Service) industries. However, the pricing range ($50–$150/month) is not clearly justified. The entrepreneurs have not provided a detailed cost structure, value proposition, or competitive pricing benchmark to support their pricing assumptions. This lack of specificity reduces the credibility of their revenue model.
- **Scalability:** The model is inherently scalable, as software solutions can serve an increasing number of customers with minimal incremental cost. However, the assumption that "one percent of independent restaurants" will adopt the product is overly optimistic and lacks data backing. The market size estimate is not substantiated with market research or industry data.
- **Alternative Revenue Streams:** The entrepreneurs mention potential future revenue streams (e.g., reports, scheduling, multi-location versions, and a percentage of additional revenue). These are promising but speculative and not yet validated. The current model is too narrow and lacks diversification.

**2. Strategy for Growth:**
- **Customer Acquisition:** The strategy to acquire customers through in-person visits, social media, partnerships, and word of mouth is low-cost but likely slow and inefficient. There is no mention of a marketing budget, customer acquisition cost (CAC), or customer lifetime value (LTV) analysis, which are critical for evaluating the effectiveness of this approach.
- **Market Fit:** The entrepreneurs assume that the problem is significant enough to justify the product, but the solution is not yet tested in real-world conditions. The prototype is based on fabricated and limited real data, which means the product's effectiveness is unproven. This undermines the assumption that the product will solve the problem as described.
- **Competitive Differentiation:** While the entrepreneurs claim to be focused on a specific niche (table turn time prediction and seating optimization), the claim that "big competitors could easily add this feature" is a valid risk. The lack of a clear, defensible competitive advantage weakens the strategy.

**3. Validity of Assumptions:**
- **Market Size:** The assumption that "one percent of independent restaurants" will adopt the product is not supported by any market research or industry data. The U.S. restaurant industry is vast, but the entrepreneurs have not quantified the number of relevant restaurants (15–60 tables) or their potential willingness to pay.
- **Customer Willingness to Pay:** The pricing range is not justified by a value proposition or cost-benefit analysis. The entrepreneurs have not demonstrated how the product reduces wait times, improves revenue, or enhances customer satisfaction in a measurable way.
- **Product Efficacy:** The product is not yet tested in real environments. The prediction model is trained on fabricated and limited data, which raises questions about its accuracy and reliability. Without real-world validation, the product's value proposition is speculative.

**Conclusion:**
The business model is viable in theory but lacks the necessary data, justification, and validation to support its assumptions. The strategy for growth is underdeveloped, and the product has not been sufficiently tested to confirm its effectiveness. The entrepreneurs have a clear vision, but they need to substantiate their claims with market research, customer validation, and a more rigorous financial model. Without these, the scalability and long-term viability of the business remain uncertain.
